title: House Robber III Problem

notes: The tree argument is serialized in level-order; null marks a missing child.
The returned value is the maximum sum of node values with no parent-child pair selected together.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Maximum amount of money the thief can rob = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
Maximum amount of money the thief can rob = 4 + 5 = 9.

content.problemStatement:
The thief has found himself a new place for his thievery again. There is only one entrance to this area, called `root`.

Besides the `root`, each house has one and only one parent house. After a tour, the smart thief realized that all houses in this place form a binary tree. It will automatically contact the police if **two directly-linked houses were broken into on the same night**.

With the `root` of the binary tree, output *the largest amount of money the thief can rob **without alerting the police***.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/03/10/rob1-tree.jpg)

```
Input: root = [3,2,3,null,3,null,1]
Output: 7
Explanation: Maximum amount of money the thief can rob = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/03/10/rob2-tree.jpg)

```
Input: root = [3,4,5,1,3,null,1]
Output: 9
Explanation: Maximum amount of money the thief can rob = 4 + 5 = 9.
```

**Constraints:**

* The number of nodes in the tree is in the range `[1, 10^4]`.
* `0 <= Node.val <= 10^4`

notes: All supported-language boilerplates use the supplied level-order JSON tree format.
Implementations are iterative where recursion depth could otherwise be problematic for a 10^4-node skewed tree.
For a node u, take[u] = u.val + skip[left] + skip[right].
solution.approach: Use postorder tree DP with two states for each node: the best sum when the node is robbed, and the best sum when the node is skipped. If the node is robbed, both children must be skipped. If it is skipped, each child may be either robbed or skipped. An explicit postorder stack keeps the reference implementation safe for highly skewed trees.

better.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memoization space.
better.description: Memoize the result of each subtree for the two possible states (whether the current node may be robbed). Each node-state is solved once, reducing repeated work and giving linear time.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space in the worst case.
optimal.description: Use bottom-up tree DP with two values per node: take and skip. A postorder traversal computes both from the children exactly once. An explicit stack avoids recursion-depth failures on a 10^4-node skewed tree.

bruteForce.complexity: O(2^n) time and O(h) recursion stack.
bruteForce.description: Try both choices for every node while enforcing that a robbed node cannot have a robbed child. The same subtrees are recomputed many times, so the running time is exponential in the number of nodes.

solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) worst case for the explicit traversal stack and per-node DP map.

followUps: Can you implement the same two-state DP recursively without a memoization table, and what is the resulting auxiliary-space complexity?
How would the approach change if each edge represented a different conflict relationship rather than only parent-child conflicts?
